title: the flute
carry: jealous of a reed, then glad

segments.voice: Yesterday, the flute: the calves stood with milk in their mouths, the birds closed their eyes, and the rivers slowed. Did any sound stop you yesterday? Day eight hundred ninety-eight.

What did a stick do to deserve this? That's the gopis' question, and they're not joking. They're still in the village, still listening, and one of them says what the others have been thinking. Krishna's lips are on that flute all day long. It's a length of bamboo, cut from some riverbank. It has no voice of its own, no family, no story. And yet it gets to be closer to him than any of them. So they ask, half in envy and half in wonder: what good thing did this flute ever do? Today the flute again, from the side of the flute.
screen: `WHAT DID A STICK DO?` → `CLOSER TO HIM THAN ANY OF THEM.` → `FROM THE SIDE OF THE FLUTE.`

segments.voice: The Bhagavata gives the question to one of the gopis. What virtue, she asks, did this flute practice, that it gets to enjoy the sweetness of his lips, a sweetness the gopis feel belongs to them, and leaves them only what's left over? Then she answers herself in a strange and lovely way. She looks at the bamboo's family. The lakes and rivers whose water raised the bamboo are glad: their lotuses open as if the hair on their skin were standing up. And the trees, the bamboo's elders, let their sap run down like tears, the way old people weep with joy when someone in the family turns out devoted. So the gopi's envy turns, halfway through her sentence, into a kind of praise. Somebody belonging to the riverbank got close to Krishna, and the whole riverbank is proud. Now look at what a flute actually is. A hollow reed. Breath goes in one end and comes out as music, and the flute adds nothing of its own except the empty space. That's the detail some devotional teachers return to: the flute is close to Krishna because there's nothing inside it in the way. They read the gopi's question as the devotee's question, what would it take for me to be that close, and the flute as the answer, a life with room in it. That's an interpretation, not a line in the chapter. The chapter itself just leaves us with a woman in a village, jealous of a piece of bamboo, and then glad for it.
screen: `WHAT GOOD DID THIS FLUTE EVER DO?` · `THE RIVERS AND TREES ARE PROUD.` · `A HOLLOW REED, EMPTY INSIDE.` · then, large: `A LIFE WITH ROOM IN IT.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably and let your shoulders drop. For these two minutes, let your breath be the only thing moving through you, the way breath moves through a reed. Breathe in without grabbing. Breathe out without pushing. Each time you exhale, let one small thing go with it: a plan, a worry, a sentence you were rehearsing. You don't have to empty everything. Just make a little room. If you pray, you can offer the room you've made to Krishna, or to God by any name you use. The bell holds the time.
The flute. A hollow length of bamboo that the gopis envy, because it is always at Krishna's lips.
Your line: jealous of a reed, then glad. Today, when you notice envy for someone, try the gopi's turn: look for one thing in their good luck you can be glad about. Day eight hundred ninety-eight.

howItsDone: Devotees sing and recite the gopis' words about the flute from the Bhagavata, and Krishna is honored under names that mean the one who holds the flute.

fork.setup: you're the gopi, jealous of a piece of bamboo that gets to be at Krishna's lips all day. what do you do with that feeling?
options: ask what the flute did to deserve it, and find its family rejoicing.
fork.reveal: she asks the question out loud, then answers by looking at the rivers and trees that raised the bamboo, and her envy turns into praise.

original.note: Hindi, from Sanskrit: the flute. Devotees call Krishna Murlidhar, the one who holds the flute.

trapdoor: what you thought: the gopis love Krishna's music.
what it means: they envy the flute itself, then end up praising it.
what a scholar hears: some devotional teachers read the hollow reed as the devotee with room inside; the chapter leaves that unsaid.

sources.ref: Bhagavata Purana 10.21, the gopis' question about the flute's good deeds and its rejoicing 'family' of rivers and trees

notes: All paraphrase. Confirm against Bhagavata 10.21 (around verse 9): the gopi asks what virtue the flute practiced to enjoy the nectar of his lips; the lakes (lotuses blooming like hair standing on end) and trees (shedding tears) rejoice as the bamboo's relatives.
The reading of the flute's hollowness as the devotee's emptiness is attributed to 'some devotional teachers' and flagged in the script as an interpretation; a Keeper may want to name a source or cut.
Original: मुरली given as Hindi with pronunciation MUR-lee; Sanskrit pronunciation differs (mu-ra-lee). A Keeper may prefer the Sanskrit form or null.
Murlidhar as a devotional name of Krishna: confirm spelling for this audience.
